metadata.note: Denver & Rio Grande / Denver and Rio Grande Western narrow-gauge San Juan Extension: Alamosa, CO - Antonito, CO - over Cumbres Pass - Chama, NM - Durango, CO, built 1878-1881. This file splits the route into three geographic segments (Alamosa-Antonito, Antonito-Chama, Chama-Durango), each further split at the 1921 D&RG-to-D&RGW reorganization per this project's ownership-change convention, plus a seventh, separate feature for the post-1970 Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad heritage tourist operation on the Antonito-Chama segment specifically. RESEARCH FINDING CONTRARY TO INITIAL ASSUMPTION: sources consulted here are consistent and specific that D&RG/D&RGW-operated THROUGH PASSENGER SERVICE (the San Juan Express and its predecessors) ended on the SAME DATE, February 1, 1951, across the entire Alamosa-Durango line -- not at different dates for Antonito-Chama vs Chama-Durango as might be expected from Chama-Durango's earlier physical abandonment (1968) and the Antonito-Chama segment's later heritage preservation (1970). After February 1951 the D&RGW's only remaining narrow-gauge passenger service anywhere on its system was the unrelated Durango-Silverton mixed train; freight (including a brief 1950s-60s Farmington-area oil/gas traffic boom) continued alone on this route until 1968. All six D&RG/D&RGW features in this file therefore share the same end year, 1951, honestly reflecting what was found rather than the initially-assumed staggered end dates. A single-car Chama-Dulce passenger train is mentioned in one source as running briefly right after the San Juan's January 1951 discontinuance; no end date for it was found, so it is not used to extend any drawn year -- see not_yet_sourced.
metadata.geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass (overpass-api.de), railway=narrow_gauge/rail/abandoned/disused ways, queried in a bbox spanning Alamosa CO to Durango CO/Chama NM. Alamosa-Antonito uses OSM's currently-active 'Alamosa-Antonio Branch'/'Alamosa-Antonio Spur' (railway=rail, the modern San Luis & Rio Grande Railroad, same alignment as the historic D&RG/D&RGW line). Antonito-Chama uses OSM's 'Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad' (railway=narrow_gauge, tagged old_railway_operator=D&RGW, railway:preserved=yes) -- the same physical track used by both the historic D&RG/D&RGW features and the modern heritage-railroad feature in this file. Chama-Durango uses OSM's 'Rio Grande Southern (Chama to Durango)' abandoned/disused ways -- this OSM name is a mistagging (the Rio Grande Southern was a different, unrelated D&RG-affiliated narrow-gauge company running Ridgway-Durango-Rico-Telluride; the tagged geometry here is geographically the D&RGW San Juan Extension grade, corroborated by mileposts, the explicit '(Chama to Durango)' name suffix, and several nearby ways independently tagged old_railway_operator=D&RGW), corrected here to the right company without otherwise altering the traced geometry. Excluded from all three traces: the Rio Grande & Southwestern Railroad (a separate lumber-company narrow gauge near Lumberton, NM), the Rio Grande, Pagosa, and Northern Railroad (the 1900-1935 Pagosa Springs branch off this line at Gato/Pagosa Junction), the Farmington Branch, the Chili Line (Antonito-Santa Fe), the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad branch, and the Alamosa-Walsenburg standard-gauge line -- all separate companies/branches sharing the Antonito or Durango yard areas. Ways were chained by a greedy nearest-endpoint algorithm per named/tagged group, then checked for self-intersection/backtracking (see each feature's geometry_quality) using cumulative along-path distance, not point index, per this project's established method.
not_yet_sourced: Antonito opening year conflict: most sources (Tracks Across Borders D&RGW history page; a general D&RGW timeline summary) say the D&RG reached Antonito in 1878. The Wikipedia Cumbres & Toltec Scenic Railroad article says track-laying reached Antonito in March 1880. This file uses 1878 (better corroborated) for the Alamosa-Antonito feature's start year; the 1880 alternative is not used.

Whether Chama-Durango passenger service really ended on the identical date as Antonito-Chama (February 1, 1951) or slightly earlier, as would be a plausible guess given Chama-Durango's much earlier ultimate abandonment (1968) -- every source found describes the San Juan Express as a single through train serving the whole Alamosa-Durango line and ending as one event; no source was found describing a separate, earlier withdrawal of Chama-Durango passenger service specifically. Treated here as ending on the same date for lack of contrary evidence.

A 'One Car Passenger Train that Ran from Chama to Dulce after San Juan Discontinuance' is mentioned (photo caption only, tracksacrossborders.com) as operating after the January 31, 1951 San Juan Express discontinuance. No start/end dates, frequency, or duration were found for this service, so it is not used to extend the drawn end year of the Chama-Durango or Antonito-Chama D&RGW features past 1951 -- if it in fact ran for a meaningful period, this file understates passenger service on that short stretch.

Freight-only abandonment/scrapping dates conflict across sources (last revenue freight late August 1968; 'last train to operate into Durango from the east' December 5-6 1968; american-rails.com says the line 'was abandoned' in 1969; drgw.net says scrapping started at Chama September 20 1970 and worked west). None of this affects any drawn year in this file since none of it is passenger service, but the conflict itself is unresolved.

Exact avg_speed_kmh/headway_min for the pre-1921 D&RG era (1878/1881-1921) on all three segments: no timetable was found for that era specifically; figures are carried forward by estimation from the 1941 San Juan Express schedule (the only real timetable found), which reflects 1930s-40s equipment/practice, not 1880s-1910s. See each feature's speed_source.

Precise start month/day for the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad's first operating season (1970 vs 1971): New Mexico's purchase-authorizing legislation was signed April 1969, Colorado's followed in 1970, and at least one source says the C&TSR itself was formally organized 'by 1971'; this file uses 1970 as the start year per the task brief and the most common 'purchased 1970, began operating excursions' phrasing, but the very first excursion season may actually have been 1971.

properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass (overpass-api.de), railway=rail ways tagged 'Alamosa-Antonio Branch' / 'Alamosa-Antonio Spur' -- the modern San Luis & Rio Grande Railroad, standard/dual-gauge freight trackage on the same alignment used by the historic D&RG/D&RGW narrow-gauge line before 20th-century gauge conversion.
properties.geometry_quality: REAL-TRACED from 37 OSM ways, greedy-chained by nearest endpoint, 48.09 km total. Checked for self-intersection/backtracking by cumulative along-path distance (project convention): zero flagged reversals or revisits found; one 227 m connector gap near Antonito yard (two adjacent spur ways not quite node-connected in OSM) is the only bridged gap over 50 m. No independent documented one-way mileage was found to cross-check against, but 48.09 km (29.9 mi) is consistent with the 28.6 mi Alamosa-Antonito milepost span shown in the 1941 San Juan Express timetable (mileposts measured from Denver, not from Alamosa, so a small difference is expected). This feature's geometry ends about 1.9 km short of where the separate Antonito-Chama feature's geometry begins, both within Antonito -- expected, since the two geometries come from different OSM source datasets (modern standard-gauge yard trackage vs. the narrow-gauge heritage line), not a tracing error. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 2 ruled segments totalling 27 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

properties.line: Denver & Rio Grande: Antonito – Chama (San Juan Extension, Cumbres Pass)
properties.speed_source: estimated: no 1881-1921 timetable found for this specific mountain-grade stretch; based on the 1941 San Juan Express's overall 22.0 mph / 35.4 km/h average (Alamosa-Durango, all stops) reduced to account for Cumbres Pass's much steeper grades and curvature versus the rest of the route, and for earlier, lighter equipment.

segments.note: San Juan Extension construction west from Antonito over 10,015 ft Cumbres Pass reached Chama, New Mexico on New Year's Eve, December 31, 1880; this segment uses 1881 as the first full year of revenue passenger service. Daily mixed/passenger service assumed by analogy with the later San Juan Express; no era-specific timetable found.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the references below cover this line/era generally, but nothing has been checked specifically against this segment's 1881 start year or its estimated daily headway.

properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass (overpass-api.de), railway=narrow_gauge ways tagged 'Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad' (old_railway_operator=D&RGW, railway:preserved=yes), plus the untagged 'Mud Tunnel'/'Rock Tunnel' portal ways and a handful of unnamed narrow_gauge ways filling short gaps between them.
properties.geometry_quality: REAL-TRACED from 45 OSM ways (46 minus one 340 m dead-end spur/wye at Osier that duplicated a point exactly at both its own start and end and was dropped), greedy-chained by nearest endpoint, then truncated at its closest approach to the geocoded Chama town center (81.8 m). 103.66 km total -- matches the documented 64-mile (103.0 km) Antonito-Chama distance to within 0.6%. Checked for self-intersection/backtracking by cumulative along-path distance: after removing the dead-end spur, zero exact-coordinate revisits and only two turns over 120 degrees remain (135 degrees near Cumbres Pass summit itself, 137 degrees on the final approach into the Chama valley) -- both are real, tight horseshoe/S-curves on this famously curvy mountain grade (verified against the underlying coordinates, not a mirrored point-for-point retrace), not tracing bugs. This is the same physical alignment traced for the separate post-1970 Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad feature in this file.

properties.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass (overpass-api.de), railway=abandoned/disused ways tagged 'Rio Grande Southern (Chama to Durango)' -- an OSM mistagging corrected here (see metadata.geometry_sources) -- plus nearby unnamed abandoned/disused/narrow_gauge ways within the corridor filling gaps, greedy-chained by nearest endpoint.
properties.geometry_quality: REAL-TRACED from 57 of 73 corridor-area OSM ways (15 unused ways were isolated, off-corridor fragments -- a separate lumber railroad near Lumberton and D&S/Silverton-branch yard trackage near Durango -- correctly excluded by the chaining algorithm), 180.32 km total after trimming a short exact-duplicate loop at the Chama end. This is noticeably longer than a straight-line Chama-Durango distance (~110 km) but is consistent with a winding river-valley narrow-gauge alignment and with documented mileposts (San Juan Extension mileposts run to about MP 452 at Durango against about MP 341 at Chama, i.e. roughly 111 miles / 179 km). Checked for self-intersection/backtracking by cumulative along-path distance: no exact-coordinate revisits found outside the expected Chama and Durango yard/wye trackage at each end (both termini had real wyes for turning trains); one exact-duplicate dead-end loop at the Chama end was found and removed (see above). Several turns over 120 degrees remain near Durango and one near MP ~410 -- inspected individually and consistent with real wye/passing-loop trackage at the Durango terminal and a genuine grade switchback east of Durango, not mirrored point-for-point retraces. IMPORTANT LATER-ALIGNMENT CAVEAT (CLAUDE.md Rule 2): roughly km 90-112 of this feature's 180 km length (near Rosa and the original townsite of Arboles, both in the San Juan River canyon) passes within 2 km of today's Navajo Reservoir. The original 1880s alignment through this stretch was flooded when Navajo Dam was completed and is now permanently submerged -- it cannot be traced from OSM, satellite imagery, or any other source consulted. The federal government relocated the line to the north side of the reservoir in 1961-62 (new service began September 13, 1962), and it is that RELOCATED, POST-1962 alignment that survives as visible grade today and is what OSM's abandoned-railway tagging (and this feature's geometry) actually follows in this stretch -- eleven years after this feature's own 1951 end-of-passenger-service date. This is used anyway, flagged honestly, because it is the best (and only) available real-terrain trace of this stretch; the true 1881-1951 alignment differs from what is drawn here in this ~20 km stretch and no substitute source was found for it.

properties.line: Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad: Antonito – Chama
properties.speed_source: estimated: published excursions cover the 64-mile (103 km) Antonito-Chama line in roughly 5.5-6 hours of train time including a lunch stop at Osier, implying a moving average in the high teens km/h; no minute-by-minute working timetable was consulted, so this is a rough estimate, not a sourced running time.

segments.note: Heritage narrow-gauge tourist operation on the Antonito-Chama segment of the old San Juan Extension, the same physical track as the D&RG/D&RGW-era features in this file. New Mexico authorized purchase of the abandoned D&RGW trackage by legislation signed April 1969; Colorado passed matching legislation in 1970; the two states' joint purchase of the 64-mile Antonito-Chama segment closed in 1970, and the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad began operating excursion trains shortly after (one source describes the railroad as formally organized 'by 1971' -- see metadata.not_yet_sourced for the exact first-season uncertainty). Runs seasonally, late May to late October as of recent years, with a train each morning from both Antonito and Chama meeting at Osier for lunch.
sources: Segment-level: start year (1970) and the joint Colorado/New Mexico state purchase are directly sourced to the Wikipedia Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad article and corroborated by american-rails.com and the Wikipedia Alamosa-Durango line article. The precise first operating season (1970 vs 1971) and current-day schedule/speed details are less firmly sourced -- see not_yet_sourced and speed_source.
